content.text: Minimal APIs aren't a toy version of controllers. They run on the same routing, middleware, dependency injection and authorization, and Microsoft recommends them for new projects. Route groups, endpoint filters, typed results and the validation built into .NET 10 give you the structure people assume only controllers have; controllers still win for a few MVC features, not for big apps in general.
A team starts a new orders service. In the design review, someone says: "Minimal APIs are fine for the prototype, but we'll switch to controllers before it goes live, or
will become a file nobody wants to open." The prototype ships, the switch never happens, and a year later the prediction has come true:
and its own hand-written checks. Minimal APIs didn't cause that. Nobody used the parts of them that keep an app organized.

The belief: minimal APIs are for demos, tutorials and three-endpoint microservices. A real application needs controllers, because only controllers give you structure, filters, validation, API documentation and testable code.
It isn't a silly belief. The name says "minimal", and the first example everyone sees is

in a single file. It also used to be partly true. Minimal APIs shipped in .NET 6 without endpoint filters, route groups or typed results; those arrived in .NET 7. Microsoft's .NET 6 guidance listed form binding among the reasons to pick controllers, and built-in validation only came with .NET 10.
Today the same docs say the opposite of the myth: for new projects, Microsoft recommends minimal APIs, and controllers are the alternative for specific needs.
Same app, a different way to declare endpoints
A minimal API isn't a lighter framework running next to ASP.NET Core.
create endpoints in the same routing system controllers use, and the

pipeline, dependency injection, logging, authentication and authorization are all shared, so an authorization policy or the exception handler behaves the same for both. What changes is how you declare an endpoint: a handler with typed parameters instead of an action method on a class.
Structure comes from groups, not from classes
A route handler can be a lambda or an ordinary method, and it doesn't have to live in
: endpoints that share a URL prefix, where anything you add to the group, such as
or a filter, applies to every endpoint in it. Groups can nest, and an empty prefix,
, applies metadata or filters without changing any route. The usual layout is one static class per feature with an extension method like

runs code before and after a handler, can read and change its arguments, and can return a response without calling the handler at all. A filter added to a group runs for every endpoint in it. That's the job action filters do in MVC, and a filter class that implements
can take services from dependency injection.
Validation and response types are built in
. Before the handler runs, it checks DataAnnotations attributes such as
on query, header and body parameters, including nested objects, and answers 400 with the errors when a rule fails. For responses,
and three things follow: the compiler rejects any other result, OpenAPI reads the possible responses from the signature without extra
calls, and a unit test can assert on the returned type.

content.text: The docs name four reasons to choose controllers: model binding extensibility (

), application parts or the application model, and OData. Most of these can be rebuilt by hand in minimal APIs, but controllers ship them. The docs also say controllers may suit large applications with complex business logic and teams fluent in MVC. That's a matter of fit and habit, not of a capability minimal APIs lack.

blocks.title: You don't have to pick one for the whole app

content.text: Controllers and minimal APIs are both endpoints, so
can live in the same app. Keep the feature that needs a custom model binder as a controller, and the rest as minimal APIs.
How to apply it in your project
If you need one of the four features above, make that part a controller. Otherwise minimal APIs fit, whatever the project size.

items.text: Minimal APIs are Microsoft's recommended default for new APIs, and they share routing, middleware, dependency injection and authorization with controllers.
Route groups and handler classes give a large API its structure; endpoint filters give it cross-cutting behavior.
provide validation, consistent errors and OpenAPI metadata, but only once you wire them.
Choose controllers for a specific MVC feature, such as a custom model binder or OData, not because an app is big.
